newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hoechst revamp said part of welcome trend.
newsitem.headline: Hoechst revamp said part of welcome trend.

text.p: German chemical and drugs group Hoechst AG's plan to to transform itself into a management holding group, in line with a nation-wide restructuring trend, is likely to be a winner with investors, analysts said Thursday.

Hoechst, along with some of Germany's leading companies is embracing the Anglo-Saxon concept of improving shareholder value, and on Wednesday unveiled a blueprint to tear down its solid but inefficient business structures.
The group plans to spin off its operative business into six separate legal entities next year leaving Hoechst AG to act merely as a strategic management holding group.

"Hoechst's decision is very welcome and part of a wider trend to increase the return on equity," said Peter Sullivan, strategist at Goldman Sachs in London, referring to similar plans at Daimler-Benz AG and utilty Veba AG .
Markets applauded Hoechst's plans by sending shares to a record high of 61.30 marks ($40.64) marks on Wednesday, largely ignoring the group's simultaneously reported weak operating business.
Betting that chief executive Juergen Dormann can pull off the restructuring to leave the group much stronger, analysts said Hoechst shares still had plenty of room to climb.
"This step could really fire up the share price," said Ronald Koehler, analyst at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
Hoechst shares have more than doubled in value since spring 1995 on expectations that Dormann will be able to push through his ambitious plans to boost shareholder value.

The company also said Hoechst AG shares will be listed on the New York Stock Exchange next fall and separate flotations of other units may follow with analysts betting drugs unit HMR will lead the way, likely to be listed as early as next year.

The listing of Hoechst AG shares will not involve raising new capital, chief financial officer Klaus Schmieder said. For the other possible flotations, Schmieder said the group had a variety of options, including raising capital or selling part of its own stake in the units.
"The step is based on an argument European chemical groups' sum of their parts may be more worth more than the whole," said Lutz Grueten, analyst at Kleinwort Benson in Frankfurt.
While Hoechst's plan is fundamentally different from carmaker Daimler-Benz's holding structure, strategists said the process barely matters as long as the results are positive.

"Companies will have separate versions but what really matters is whether the changes will contribute to returns on equity," Goldman's Sullivan said, predicting other European companies will follow suit, realising U.S. groups already gained.

In a Goldman Sachs study, the investment bank said U.S. companies on average boosted their return on equity by three percent with such steps and predicted German companies stand to boost their own return on equity by about two percent.
But analysts disagree over how quickly other German companies, particularly in the chemical and drugs market will overhaul their structures.

"In the medium term I believe Hoechst will be the only group to pull this kind of restructuring off in this way," said Kleinwort's Grueten, adding this will be a one factor why Hoechst could outperform its rivals.
"The market has shown it does not love conglomerates and prefers strategically focused companies," he added.
Goldman Sachs' Sullivan however added more and more companies will experiment with new models.
"The pressure will be on any company needing to raise capital," he said. ($ = 1.508 German Marks)
